claims.measure: allogrooming, social dominance, pup ultrasonic vocalisation

claims.text: Shank3 recruits ABI1 and the WAVE complex to the postsynaptic density, a function independent of its binding to GKAP and Homer.
claims.limO: Independence from GKAP and Homer binding is asserted in the abstract without the supporting comparison being described.
claims.model: biochemical and cellular analysis plus knock-in mouse
claims.measure: recruitment of ABI1 and the WAVE complex to the postsynaptic density

claims.text: Shank3+/dC mice showed reduced probability and smaller amplitude of conditioned eyeblink responses, aberrant response timing and reduced Purkinje cell dendritic spine density.
claims.limO: No n or statistics in the abstract. Five models are compared without a stated correction for multiple comparisons.
claims.model: Shank3+/dC, one of five autism-related models compared
claims.measure: delay eyeblink conditioning; Purkinje cell dendritic spine density

claims.text: Sleep disruption during adolescence, but not during adulthood, caused long-lasting impairment of social novelty preference in mice.
claims.limO: The adulthood arm is a null reported without power or confidence interval, so the age specificity rests on a failure to detect in one arm.
claims.model: wild-type mice subjected to sleep disruption
claims.measure: social novelty preference after sleep disruption

claims.text: In Shank3-mutant mice, improving sleep or rectifying ventral tegmental area activity during adolescence ameliorated adult social deficits.
claims.limO: Neither the allele, nor n, nor the magnitude of improvement is given in the abstract. 'Ameliorated' is not quantified.
claims.model: Shank3-mutant mice; allele not specified in the abstract
claims.measure: adult social behaviour

claims.text: Chemogenetic activation of prefrontal cortex pyramidal neurons restored social preference behaviour and elevated glutamatergic synaptic function in Shank3-deficient mice.
claims.limO: No n, no effect size. A chemogenetic manipulation is not a candidate human intervention; it localises a circuit rather than proposing a treatment.
claims.model: Shank3-deficient mice; allele not specified in the abstract
claims.measure: social preference; glutamatergic synaptic function

claims.text: Blocking Sgk function in Shank3-deficient mice prevented chemogenetic prefrontal activation from rescuing social and synaptic deficits.
claims.limO: A blocked rescue is uninterpretable without evidence that the inhibitor did not simply impair the animals independently; the abstract does report that blocking Sgk in wild-types induced social deficits, which is exactly that confound.
claims.model: Shank3-deficient mice
claims.measure: social behaviour and glutamatergic synaptic function

claims.text: Shank3 deletion preferentially affected synapses onto striatopallidal medium spiny neurons, which showed altered synaptic transmission, plasticity and spine density.

conflicts.title: Does sleep disturbance differ between SHANK3 sequence variants and 22q13 deletions?
conflicts.summary: Two reports of the same comparison give point estimates in the same direction but opposite conclusions. One reports sleep disturbance in 89% of people with a SHANK3 pathogenic variant against 59.6% with a deletion and treats this as a difference. The other reports 84.8% against 71.9% and describes the two as similarly frequent, then uses that similarity as positive evidence for SHANK3 haploinsufficiency driving sleep problems.
candidate_explanations: Different cohorts: a clinically ascertained series versus an international registry, with different ascertainment of both genotype and sleep.
Neither comparison is reported with a statistical test, a confidence interval or an equivalence margin, so neither 'difference' nor 'similarity' is established.
Sleep is measured by caregiver report in both, with no stated instrument equivalence.
conflicts.group_note: Both reports share authorship. This is a group reaching different conclusions from the same comparison in two datasets, not two groups disagreeing.
conflicts.why_it_matters: A difference by genotype class would mean sleep is partly driven by genes other than SHANK3 in the deleted region, and therefore not fully correctable by restoring SHANK3. Sleep is also among the endpoints most often proposed for trials and most tracked by families.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: A single prospectively defined comparison of sleep in SHANK3 sequence-variant versus deletion groups, using the same instrument in both, with the sample size fixed in advance to detect a stated minimum difference, and an equivalence margin declared before analysis so that a null can mean something.

conflicts.title: Does deletion size relate to phenotype severity?
conflicts.summary: One cohort of 15 individuals, deeply phenotyped, finds no relation between deletion size and severity. A separate cohort of 51 places the individuals with the largest mutation (7.23 Mb) in the cluster with the greatest impairment.
candidate_explanations: Sample size: 15 versus 51. The smaller study is underpowered to detect a relation whether or not one exists, and reports no statistics at all.
Different phenotype measures and different analytic approaches: a direct size-severity correlation versus hierarchical clustering.
Deletion size is a crude proxy for gene content; two deletions of similar length need not remove the same genes.
conflicts.why_it_matters: This is the single most load-bearing question for the premise of SHANK3 restoration. If severity tracks deletion size, part of the phenotype is driven by neighbouring genes and could not be normalised by restoring SHANK3 alone. Several studies in this corpus conclude the opposite from underpowered nulls.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: A pooled analysis across existing registries with gene content rather than deletion length as the predictor, a prespecified severity measure, and sufficient individuals at each deletion size. The gene-level table this project is building is a prerequisite rather than an afterthought.

conflicts.title: Do heterozygous Shank3 mice show behavioural deficits?
conflicts.summary: One source states that heterozygous deletion of Shank3 in mice does not commonly induce ASD-related behavioural deficits. Another reports that heterozygous exon 4-9 deletion mice show increased repetitive grooming, object recognition deficits, abnormal ultrasonic vocalisations and a reduced NMDA/AMPA ratio at striatal synapses.
candidate_explanations: Different alleles: an unspecified heterozygous deletion versus a defined exon 4-9 deletion. Shank3 has multiple intragenic promoters and isoforms, so different deletions remove different protein products.
Genetic background differences, which are known to modify Shank3 phenotypes.
The first statement is made as background about a literature rather than as a result, and carries no supporting data.
conflicts.why_it_matters: People with PMS are heterozygous. If heterozygous mice show little or allele-dependent phenotype, then most preclinical evidence supporting candidate treatments is being generated in homozygous animals, a genotype no patient has. That affects how preclinical efficacy should be read.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: A head-to-head comparison of several heterozygous Shank3 alleles on one genetic background, in one laboratory, with a prespecified behavioural battery, adequate power and effect sizes reported for each allele.

conflicts.title: Are activity and impulsivity elevated in PMS?
conflicts.summary: An independent group comparing 30 individuals with PMS against matched fragile X, Down syndrome and idiopathic autism samples found no differences in impulsivity or overactivity, contrary to the position of the prior behavioural phenotype literature. The instruments did detect other group differences, so this is not a blanket insensitivity.
candidate_explanations: The prior literature is cited generically in the abstract, with no specific study named, so the exact claim being tested is not pinned down.
Comparison against other genetic syndromes rather than against typical development changes what counts as elevated.
Different instruments across the earlier and later work.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Hyperactivity and impulsivity appear in clinical descriptions of PMS and shape what families and clinicians expect. If the elevation is relative to typical development but not to other syndromes, the phenotype is less specific than it is usually presented.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: Direct comparison using the same instrument against both a typically developing group and at least one other genetic syndrome group, with the prior finding named and its effect size stated as the target to be reproduced.

conflicts.title: What is the repetitive behaviour profile in PMS?
conflicts.summary: The same independent comparison found compulsive and routine-driven repetitive behaviours less common in PMS than in the comparison groups, with elevation confined to motor stereotypies, against an earlier description of a repetitive-behaviour profile resembling idiopathic autism.
candidate_explanations: Repetitive behaviour is not one construct: motor stereotypy and compulsive or routine-driven behaviour can dissociate, and instruments differ in how they weight them.
Developmental level differs between PMS and the comparison groups and strongly affects compulsive behaviour.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Repetitive behaviour is a common outcome measure in trials. If the profile in PMS is predominantly motor stereotypy rather than compulsive behaviour, a scale weighted towards the latter would be measuring the wrong thing.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: Component-level analysis of repetitive behaviour in PMS against matched groups, adjusted for developmental level, reporting subscales separately rather than a total score.

conflicts.title: Are social and repetitive phenotypes in Shank3 mutant mice reproducible?
conflicts.summary: Across three independently bred cohorts of Shank3 ankyrin-domain mutant mice, repetitive self-grooming, reduced ultrasonic vocalisations and water-maze reversal deficits appeared in some cohorts and not others, and adult three-chambered sociability was normal in all genotypes. This stands against the robust social-interaction and self-grooming phenotype reported for the Shank3B exon 13-16 allele by another laboratory.
candidate_explanations: Different alleles: an ankyrin-repeat mutation versus an exon 13-16 deletion. This is a boundary condition rather than a head-to-head refutation.
Cohort-to-cohort variation within one laboratory, which is itself the finding and points to uncontrolled environmental or husbandry variables.
Three-chambered sociability is a single assay with known sensitivity to testing conditions.
conflicts.group_note: The inconsistency across cohorts is internal to one laboratory; the comparison against the Shank3B phenotype is across groups.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Social deficit in Shank3 mice is the endpoint on which most preclinical rescue claims rest. If it varies between cohorts of the same line, a rescue measured in one cohort may not be a rescue.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: A multi-site study of the same alleles with a common protocol, reporting cohort as a factor and publishing per-cohort effect sizes rather than pooled means.

conflicts.title: Is striatal volume increased or decreased in PMS?
conflicts.summary: Relative volumes of caudate, putamen and left pallidum were decreased in people with PMS against matched controls, the opposite direction to the striatal hypertrophy that mouse models had established as the expected neuroanatomical change.
candidate_explanations: Species difference, which is the most likely explanation and is itself worth establishing.
Relative rather than absolute volumes, which depend on total brain volume.
Age: mouse findings come from young animals, the human series spans a wider range.
Small human sample and controls drawn from a separate study.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Neuroimaging is repeatedly proposed as a PMS biomarker. A measure that moves in opposite directions in the model and in patients cannot serve as a translational readout until the discrepancy is explained, and it is a concrete instance of the mouse-to-human divergence flagged elsewhere in this corpus.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: Age-matched volumetry in patients and in a Shank3 model with the same analysis pipeline and absolute rather than relative volumes, including a developmental time course in both.

conflicts.title: Is tactile reactivity in PMS reduced or heightened?
conflicts.summary: A Spanish cohort of 51 genetically confirmed patients reports definite differences associated with tactile hyperreactivity, against an earlier described PMS profile of underresponsiveness, sensation-seeking and tactile hyporeactivity.
candidate_explanations: Different instruments: parent-report questionnaire versus clinician-administered observation, which is a sufficient explanation on its own.
Different age distributions.
Sensory profiles are known to include both hypo- and hyper-reactivity in the same individual, so a summary direction may be an artefact of scoring.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Tactile reactivity is proposed both as an outcome measure and, in animal work, as a developmental driver of social behaviour. Its direction in PMS needs to be settled before it can serve as either.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: Administration of both the parent-report and the clinician-administered instruments to the same individuals, reporting hypo- and hyper-reactivity subscales separately and their agreement.

conflicts.title: Do different Shank2 alleles give opposite synaptic phenotypes?
conflicts.summary: A direct comparison of two independently generated Shank2 knockout lines found different sets of synaptic phenotypes, with enhanced long-term potentiation in one line, which the authors state runs contrary to prior work on SHANK protein function. Both phenotypes are concluded to be real and background-dependent.
candidate_explanations: Different exons removed, producing different residual protein products.
Genetic background and modifier genes, which the authors themselves propose.
This is a jointly run comparison rather than an adversarial replication, so the two results were generated under shared conditions.
conflicts.group_note: Authors from both originating laboratories appear on the comparison, which strengthens it as a controlled comparison and weakens it as independent replication.
conflicts.why_it_matters: It concerns SHANK2 rather than SHANK3, but it demonstrates that within a single SHANK gene, allele construction and genetic background can reverse the direction of a core synaptic readout. That is a direct caution for how SHANK3 allele differences are interpreted throughout this corpus.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: Backcrossing both alleles onto a common background and repeating the synaptic measurements blind to genotype, with the residual protein products characterised by isoform-specific antibodies.

conflicts.title: How frequent are SHANK3 structural variants in idiopathic autism?
conflicts.summary: Copy number analysis of SHANK3, SHANK2, NLGN3 and NLGN4 in 285 Chinese autism cases detected no deletion or duplication in any of the four genes, against reported occurrence of such variants in autism.
candidate_explanations: Underpowered by construction: at a reported SHANK3 structural variant frequency of roughly 0.5 to 1% in autism, the expected count in 285 cases is one to three, so observing zero is compatible with the published frequency.
Population differences in variant frequency.
Assay sensitivity for small intragenic events.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Included as a worked example rather than as a real conflict: this is what an underpowered null looks like when it is framed as a failure to reproduce. It should not be cited as a refutation, and the catalogue says so.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: None required. The observation is consistent with the prior frequency estimate; a test would need several thousand cases to distinguish the hypotheses.

conflicts.title: Does environmental enrichment benefit Shank3 model animals?
conflicts.summary: Early environmental enrichment produced no benefit in Shank3 complete knockout mice, with no change in repetitive self-grooming or hole-board exploration, against a literature in which enrichment benefits ASD-like phenotypes relatively consistently across rodent models.
candidate_explanations: A conceptual rather than direct replication: prior reports used other models and no single protocol is repeated.
Enrichment protocol choice, which the authors themselves name as an untested alternative explanation.
Complete knockout rather than the heterozygous genotype of patients.
conflicts.why_it_matters: Bears directly on the plasticity-window hypothesis, that a restoration therapy combined with intensive learning or enrichment would outperform the therapy alone. It should be read against the records in this corpus where early swimming improved behaviour in a Shank3 knockout rat and where improving adolescent sleep ameliorated adult social deficits in a Shank3 model. The three together suggest the benefit depends on what the enrichment consists of.
conflicts.resolving_experiment: A single study comparing enrichment, exercise and sleep interventions against each other in the same Shank3 line and age window, with the components separated rather than bundled, and handling controlled.
